\[
\hat{I} = \operatorname{ISWT}\big(a_J,\ \eta_T(h_j),\ \eta_T(v_j),\ \eta_T(d_j)\big),
\quad
\big(a_J,\ (h_j, v_j, d_j)_{j=1}^{J}\big) = \operatorname{SWT}(I),
\qquad
\hat{I}_{\text{cycle}} = \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{s} S_{-s}\, \operatorname{IDWT}\big(\eta_T(\operatorname{DWT}(S_s I))\big),
\quad
J = 3,\ n = 4
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(I\): The input channel
- \(a_J\): The approximation after J levels
- \(h_j, v_j, d_j\): The horizontal, vertical and diagonal details of level j. Level 1 is the finest.
- \(\eta_T\): The shrink rule with threshold T
- \(S_s\): A circular shift by s = (s_y, s_x) pixels
- \(n\): The number of shifts in each direction for cycle spinning
- \(T\): The threshold, in pixel values

The decimated transform keeps every second coefficient at each level, so its result changes when the image moves by one pixel. The stationary transform, after Nason and Silverman, skips the subsampling. At level j its filters have 2^(j-1) - 1 zeros between their taps, so each subband has one coefficient per pixel. The thresholds, the noise estimate and the shrink rule eta_T are those of wavelet thresholding, applied to these coefficients. White noise keeps its sigma in every subband, since the filters have unit energy. Coifman and Donoho called this translation-invariant denoising. They showed that it equals cycle spinning over all shifts: shift the image by s, threshold it with the decimated transform, shift it back by -s, and average. S_s shifts by s in a circle. With J levels, 2^J shifts in each direction cover all the cases. Cycle spinning with fewer shifts averages only some of them.
